transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Well, I suppose what finally pushed me to come in is this habit I have of not staying seated when I’m meant to. In meetings at school, or even at dinner, everyone else will be sitting there, and I’ll suddenly be up—refilling coffee, checking a handout, walking to the back of the room—when really, it isn’t urgent at all.

It sounds small, I know, but it keeps happening, and I’ve started to feel a bit embarrassed by it.
Do you often feel restless or have a strong urge to move, even when you're trying to stay still?

Yes, I do. It’s not always dramatic, but I notice it when I’m supposed to be still. If I’m sitting at my desk grading essays, I’ll be tapping my foot or clicking my pen before I even realize I’m doing it. Same thing in church—I’ll shift around in the pew, then catch myself and think, “For heaven’s sake, just sit still.”

It reminds me a bit of when I used to tell my students not to drum on the desks, and now here I am doing my own little version of it. I can usually stop for a while if I make myself, but then a few minutes later I’m moving again.
Do you often find it hard to focus on tasks or conversations, even when you're trying to pay attention?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I do have moments where I lose the thread of what someone’s saying, but then again, don’t we all? Especially if the conversation goes on a bit—staff meetings can be endless, you know, with everyone discussing timetables and exam boards.

Sorry, I’m wandering off. I suppose I haven’t really noticed focus being the main problem. It’s more that I’m aware of myself getting uncomfortable sitting there, if that makes sense.
Do you often feel anxious or worried about things in general, even when there’s no immediate reason to be?

I don’t know that I’d call myself anxious in general. I mean, I worry about ordinary things—whether I’ve marked papers properly, whether I’ve remembered to send an email, that sort of thing. Though honestly, the email system at school is a nuisance, and half the time people don’t read them anyway.

But no, I don’t think I’m sitting around worried for no reason most of the time. At least, that’s not what I’ve noticed.
Have you noticed feeling down, depressed, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even if just for a few days?

I’m not sure I’ve really noticed that, no. I mean, I have off days, of course—who doesn’t? Sometimes after a long week at school I don’t feel like doing much, but that might just be tiredness, or age, or the weather. This time of year especially, when it gets dark early, everyone seems a bit flat.

But losing interest in things I enjoy… I don’t think so. I still like my usual bits and pieces, when I get around to them. So, no, I wouldn’t say I’ve felt depressed, not in any clear way.
Do you find yourself starting tasks but not finishing them, or having trouble organizing things even when you intend to?

I don’t think so, not in any dramatic way. I mean, I do start things and then get interrupted, but at school that’s half the job, isn’t it? You go to sort one stack of papers and then someone knocks on the door about a missing textbook, and then there’s a bell, and then—well, the whole day gets chopped up.

At home, perhaps I leave a few things half-done now and then, but I wouldn’t say I’ve really noticed a big problem with finishing or organizing. Though my desk can look terrible by Friday, but I know where things are… mostly.
Do you find yourself often missing details or making careless mistakes in your work or daily tasks, even when you're trying to be careful?

I wouldn’t say often, no. I mean, everyone makes the odd mistake, don’t they? I might miss a typo on a worksheet or put something in the wrong pile now and again, especially when the photocopier’s jammed and there are three pupils waiting at the door—actually, that photocopier has been dreadful lately.

But if you mean careless mistakes all the time, even when I’m really trying, I haven’t noticed that as a particular problem. At least, no one’s pointed it out to me in that way.
Looking back, were there times in your school years when you struggled to follow through on instructions or keep your workspace organized, even when you wanted to?

Oh, school years… that’s going back a bit. I honestly don’t know. I was at school in a very different era, you know—desks in rows, very strict teachers, exercise books covered in brown paper. Funny what you remember.

I don’t particularly remember struggling with instructions. If anything, you just did what you were told, or tried to. As for keeping things organized, I’m sure my desk or bag wasn’t perfect—whose was?—but I can’t say I remember it being a real issue. It’s not something that stands out to me.

Do you notice these restlessness or movement issues only in certain places, like at school or home, or do they happen in multiple settings, such as in meetings, at home, and in other social situations?

Yes, it’s not just one place, I don’t think. It’s come up in meetings at school, certainly—that’s actually one of the things that made me come in. I’ll be sitting there with everyone else, and then I’m up refilling coffee or checking a handout or walking to the back of the room, and it’s not as though there’s a fire, you know?

And at dinner too, even at home or with other people, I’ll suddenly feel I should get up and fetch something or straighten something. Though sometimes there really is something to fetch—my husband always leaves the salt in the oddest place—but yes, I suppose it happens in more than one setting.
Looking back, were you someone who was often restless or had trouble sitting still when you were a child, maybe in school or at home?

Yes, I think I probably was. It’s funny, because I wouldn’t have called it “restless” at the time, but my old reports used to say things like, “bright girl, but needs to stay in her seat,” or “must learn to wait her turn.” My mother used to laugh about it—well, half laugh, half despair—and say I’d worn a path in the floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten.

Actually, those old pencil sharpeners with the little metal handle—do you remember them? They were bolted to the wall, and everyone queued up. I loved having an excuse to get up. But yes, looking back, I suppose I was that child who was up and down when I probably should’ve been sitting still.
Have these restlessness and movement issues caused you any significant problems in your work, relationships, or other important areas of your life?

Yes… I think it has, though I don’t like admitting that. It’s not ruining my life, exactly, but it has started to affect things.

At work, in meetings, people do lose patience with me a bit. I can see it on their faces when I’m up and down or shifting about—there’s this look of, “Can you just sit still for five minutes?” And our staff meetings are already long enough, honestly, especially when someone starts discussing photocopier policy as if it’s a matter of national importance… sorry, that’s not really the point.

The point is, I leave feeling embarrassed. Same with book club in the community. I go because I want to feel connected to people, but sometimes I come away feeling I’ve irritated everyone rather than enjoyed the evening. So yes, it’s causing problems socially and at work, not dramatically, but enough that I notice it.
Have there been times when your restlessness or difficulty staying seated was much worse, or seemed to come on suddenly, in response to feeling down or stressed?

I’m not sure I can pin it to that, really. I mean, stress probably makes everything feel more noticeable—if I’ve had a difficult day, I’m sure I’m less patient with myself and everyone else.

But I don’t remember it suddenly appearing because I was down or upset, if that’s what you mean. It’s more… just sort of there, across ordinary days too. Though now I’m thinking about exam season at school, and the staffroom during exam season is like a pressure cooker—everyone guarding the biscuits and complaining about timetables—so perhaps I move about more then, but I couldn’t honestly say it comes on suddenly because of mood.
Do you find it especially hard to focus during tasks that require a lot of attention or mental effort, like reading through a long report or preparing a lesson plan?

I’m not sure, really. I mean, long reports are nobody’s idea of a good time, are they? Especially the ones from the council with twelve pages of wording where three would have done. I do sometimes have to make myself sit down and get through them, but I don’t know that it’s especially worse for me than for anyone else.

Lesson plans… well, after this many years teaching, some of it is almost muscle memory, though of course they keep changing the templates, which is its own small form of punishment. Sorry—yes, focus. I suppose I haven’t really noticed that as the main problem. It’s not something I’d immediately point to and say, “That’s the issue.”
